background.definition: The World Health Organization defines geographic tongue, also known as , as an irregularly shaped localized absence of filiform papillae of the tongue which changes its location over time.

list.listitem: Point prevalence of geographic tongue in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III population for adults was 1.8% (18/1000) and for children was 1% (10/1000). A slightly higher worldwide point prevalence of 3% (95% CI -0.2% to 5.5%, n = 10,967) was reported in a meta-analysis of 8 studies.
In a cross-sectional study of the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966, the prevalence of geographic tongue was 0.9%.
In a Brazilian cross-sectional study of 541 preschoolers of low socioeconomic status, 2.8% had geographic tongue.

Overall relative frequency of geographic tongue in children was 1.3% (pooled frequency 2.1; 95% CI 1.3-3.0) based on a recent scoping review of global and regional cases of oral mucosal disorders in over 85,000 children identified from clinical studies and biopsy records.
Among pregnant women, geographic tongue was identified in 2.8% making it the 5th most common oral mucosal disorder based on a systematic review of 15 studies with 5935 women.
Anxiety level, based on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, was significantly higher in individuals with geographic tongue compared to a control group.

In a case-control study, 9 of 60 patients (15%) with geographic tongue were positive for IgA tissue transglutaminase antibodies, and, in those patients, histological changes consistent with celiac disease were confirmed by duodenal biopsy vs. no patients in the control group. Only two of the 9 reported gastrointestinal symptoms.

Other conditions associated with geographic tongue are autoimmune diseases (6.7% vs. 0%), iron-deficiency anemia (18.3% vs. 0%), asthma (10% vs. 0%), and psoriasis (12% vs. 3% among healthy controls). In a case-control study of patients with psoriasis, however, fissured tongue and cigarette smoking were associated with psoriasis but not geographic tongue, which was present in 2.3% of both groups.
Etiology of geographic tongue is unknown, though genetics, fissured tongue, atopy, stress, and psoriasis may be partially causative.
In an Italian case series of 137 patients with geographic tongue, 33.6% had a family history of geographic tongue.
Family and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) studies suggest polygenic heredity. In a recent case series, HLA-B*58 was associated with geographic tongue.

Inflammation likely plays a role. Some cases of geographic tongue are caused by IL36RN mutations. In other patients in this case series, geographic tongue was associated with an imbalance in expression between IL-36Ra and IL-36γ proteins in tongue tissue. Impaired inflammatory regulation, manifesting as increased levels of soluble bacterial pattern recognition receptor (sCD14) in saliva of patients with geographic tongue vs. controls, was found in one small study.
In a case-control study, polymorphisms in the 5HTT gene were associated with geographic tongue.
May be associated with HIV and rarely with chronic lithium use.
Drugs associated with geographic tongue include angiogenesis inhibitors such as bevacizumab, and venetoclax, which is used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Characteristic lesion derives appearance from a central area of healing, consisting of a subepithelial area with evidence of chronic inflammation, an intact basal cell layer, and thinned epithelium without differentiation to filiform papillae or normal keratinization.
The whitish border, the active edge of the lesion, is composed of leukocyte infiltration, microabscess formation, intracellular edema, and exfoliation of necrotic surface cells.

The inflammatory mediator interleukin-8 appears to contribute to the inflammatory response in geographic tongue. In addition, immunostaining of interleukin 6, 17, and 23 were similar in geographic tongue and psoriasis. Also supporting geographic tongue as an inflammatory disorder is a case-control study demonstrating elevated salivary calprotectin output among cases vs. controls and a positive correlation between levels of salivary calprotectin and number of oral lesions among cases.
Elevated levels of salivary immunoglobulin E were identified in 30 high school students with geographic tongue compared to 30 controls.

Consider diagnosis with multiple painless, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with yellowish-white serpiginous or "geographic" borders on the dorsum of the tongue which change over days to hours. C
No routine tests are required. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Grooves and fissures on the dorsum of the tongue, often with mildly atrophic papillae.
Risk factors for candidiasis and painful or burning lesions. Positive KOH or fungal culture and response to antifungal therapy.
Older patients, often smoking history; white lesion which does not change over time.
Appropriate history, no lesion migration and prompt resolution with healing.
Lacy white or erosive lesions typically on the buccal mucosa, but may be on tongue. Erosive lesions painful. Distinctive histology on biopsy.
Rare. Erythematous plaques sometimes with a white scaly surface; may accompany cutaneous psoriasis.
Oral lesions may resemble geographic tongue. Clinical triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis accompany.

list.listitem: Normally found on routine examination in an asymptomatic patient; appearance of the lesions is usually diagnostic. Some patients report pain or a burning sensation.

Inquire about oral discomfort, dry mouth or other skin lesions; prior similar lesions, recent oral trauma, environmental stress, use of antibiotics or corticosteroids, risk factors for HIV or immunodeficiency, history of diabetes, and family history of oral lesions.
Examine entire oral mucosa and skin for evidence of other lesions.
Usually appears as multiple painless, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with yellowish-white serpiginous or "geographic" borders on the dorsum of the tongue.
Appearance changes over days, sometimes hours.
Similar lesions may occur on the ventral surface of the tongue, labial, buccal, or gingival mucosa; rarely can found on the soft and hard palate.

A geographic tongue severity score based on erythema (absent to severe), white halo (absent to very thick), and area of involvement (0% to 100%) was found to have low variability and high intra- and interrater correlations among 3 experts. This may be useful for management decisions or monitoring.

In a study of 96 patients with geographic tongue, 39 (41%) also had psoriasis, of whom 26 (67%) were men. Almost half (47%) of all patients reported a burning sensation and most (75%) of the 96 patients also had fissured tongue. Fewer patients with concomitant psoriasis had oral symptoms (20% vs. 65%).
No routine tests are required.
Skin scraping and KOH smear or fungal culture may exclude candidal infection when pain or risk factors such as immunosuppression suggest this diagnosis.
Consider biopsy in doubtful cases (eg, if lichen planus or leukoplakia are suspected).

Use of a VELscope, a handheld device emitting blue light used to identify precancerous and cancerous oral lesions, was not sufficiently accurate to differentiate dysplastic from inflammatory oral lesions.
Diagnosis is typically based on the characteristic appearance of a painless lesion on the tongue.
Evaluation for oral candidiasis or biopsy can be considered in selected patients.
Treatment is not usually required.
Other than reassurance about the condition's generally benign but often persistent course, treatment is not usually required. B
Oral rinses with diphenhydramine syrup or steroid solutions, topical 0.1% tacrolimus, and topical application of 7% salicylic acid in 70% alcohol are possibly effective. C
Avoidance of spicy, acidic, or hot foods may be helpful for symptomatic patients. C
Treatment normally is not usually required.
Small case series indicate that oral rinses with diphenhydramine syrup or steroid solutions and topical application of 7% salicylic acid in 70% alcohol are possibly effective.

In one case report, topical 0.1% tacrolimus was of benefit. In a retrospective case series of 20 symptomatic patients, use of twice daily 2-minute swish-swallow with 1 mg tacrolimus capsule in 500 mL of water in addition to their current regiment or co-administration with clotrimazole troches (10 mg) or gabapentin (100-200 mg daily) resulted in improvement in 14 (70%).

Authors of a systematic review found 11 studies with 150 patients of which only one was of high quality. The most common treatments, documented in two studies each, were triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, topical tacrolimus 0.1%, topical diphenhydramine, and nutritional supplements.

Although authors of a case series of 23 patients with symptomatic geographic tongue reported benefit with an aspirin-ethanol mixture with 21 (91.3%) patients becoming asymptomatic at 3 months, investigators performing a crossover trial of patient-applied 7% salicylic acid in 70% alcohol found no benefit.

In an RCT of 28 patients with symptomatic geographic tongue, 10-day treatment with combination triamcinolone and retinoic acid was no more effective than triamcinolone alone; patients in both groups showed symptomatic improvement.
Pregabalin 25 mg twice daily was used successfully in one patient with polymyositis who was taking corticosteroids and azathioprine.

Among 29 patients with plaque psoriasis and geographic tongue treated with the IL-17 blocker secukinumab, tongue lesion severity improved although there was no correlation between change in psoriasis area severity and geographic tongue severity.
Avoidance of spicy, acidic, or hot foods may be helpful for symptomatic patients.

Photobiomodulation is a form of light therapy utilizing non-ionizing light sources such as lasers, light emitting diodes, and/or broadband light to treat oral lesions including geographic tongue; supporting data are limited. In an RCT of 50 patients with symptomatic geographic tongue, treatment with photobiomodulation of low-level laser therapy resulted in less pain, less burning sensation, and better healing with statistically significant differences at time 2 and 3 of the follow-up period compared to the control group.
Geographic tongue is a benign condition which is not contagious and does not require investigation for underlying disease. C
Inform patients that individual lesions advance and regress over hours or days, but the condition itself may last for months and even years. C
No additional follow-up is necessary. C
Geographic tongue is a benign condition which is not contagious and does not signal more serious underlying disease.
Individual lesions advance and regress over hours to days, but the condition itself may last for months or years.
Avoiding spicy, hot, or acidic foods may helpful in reducing symptoms in selected patients.
Treatments are available for painful sensations but treatment effectiveness is largely unknown.
